title: iShares U.S. Energy ETF Research Report
name: iShares U.S. Energy ETF
tagline: IYE is a capped, market-cap-weighted basket of about 40 US oil, gas and energy companies, and ExxonMobil and Chevron make up close to 40% of it. The 2026 US–Iran conflict sent oil above $100 and the fund up about 40% in a year. It has given back part of that gain as Brent slid toward $95 this month.

chapters.title: What IYE is and where it came from
chapters.lede: IYE is one of the oldest US sector ETFs. It launched in 2000 as one of the first iShares sector funds, and it now tracks the Russell 1000 Energy RIC 22.5/45 Capped Index. Under that index's caps no single stock can exceed 22.5%, and stocks above 4.5% can't together exceed 45%. Those limits matter when two companies dominate the sector.

items: iShares launches the fund as one of its first US sector ETFs, then tracking a Dow Jones energy index.
Crude spikes and then crashes in the financial crisis, and energy stocks fall with it.
US shale floods the market, OPEC fights for market share, and oil falls below $30.
COVID demand collapses, WTI futures briefly trade below zero, and IYE hits its low.
Russia invades Ukraine, oil and gas prices surge, and producers turn to buybacks and dividends.
Oil settles at $60–90. OPEC+ restraint and capital discipline keep producer profits high.
EIA and the big banks forecast Brent at $55–60 for 2026 as OPEC+ unwinds its cuts.
Hostilities begin, Strait of Hormuz traffic is disrupted in March, and Brent spikes above $110. Some reports put the peak above $120.
US strikes on Iranian tankers push Brent above $100 again. Exxon and Chevron hit 52-week highs, and IYE peaks in October.
Brent loses about 16% in a week and trades near $95. Goldman sees $78 by the end of 2027.
About 41; the top 15 are about 83% of assets (Sep 30, 2026)
Other energy sector ETFs track similar baskets at lower fees, so IYE's 0.38% is on the high side

chapters.title: What's inside
chapters.lede: In practice IYE is a bet on the integrated oil majors with a tail of exploration and production companies, refiners, pipelines and oil-service firms. Its two biggest holdings make up almost 40% of the fund.

items.title: Integrated majors
items.text: Their production, refining and chemicals businesses partly cushion swings in oil prices, and they pay steady dividends.

blocks.html: Concentration check: owning IYE is largely owning Exxon and Chevron. If you already hold either one, IYE adds less diversification than its 41 names suggest.

chapters.title: Year by year
chapters.lede: Energy is a boom-and-bust sector. Its strong years come when oil spikes (2021–22, 2026), and it lags badly when oil is in surplus.

chapters.lede: IYE's chart tracks the oil price closely: the 2020 crash, the 2022 surge, a long plateau, then the 2026 spike and this month's pullback. Hover over the line, switch to the S&P 500 comparison, or click an event.

chapters.title: What drives it: the macro story
chapters.lede: Six forces explain most of what energy stocks do. In 2026, geopolitics overwhelmed everything else. Tap a card for the current read on each.

items: About a fifth of the world's oil passes through Hormuz, and the 2026 conflict disrupted it.
Shipping disruptions in the strait remain the main upside risk to oil prices in 2027, even as peace talks progress.
Late-2025 forecasts expected OPEC+ to add close to 1 million barrels a day in the second half of 2026, mainly from Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
If peace holds and those barrels arrive, the market could swing back toward the surplus forecasters expected before the war.
EIA expected Brent at about $55 and BofA about $60 for 2026. Instead it spent much of the year above $90.
Goldman's latest call is $78 by the end of 2027. Even that would be a big drop from today.
Since 2021, US producers have held back on growth spending and returned cash to shareholders.
High prices with steady spending means very large free cash flow, which supports the stocks even if oil eases.
Data-center and AI power demand is lifting US natural-gas demand.
Fidelity favored lower-cost producers with exposure to power demand, while Morningstar named Devon, Energy Transfer and Antero among its top picks.
Integrated majors and refiners hit highs, while oil-services names like SLB lagged the commodity.
That spread is a reason to look at what's inside an energy ETF, not just the oil price.

chapters.title: Why it's on the radar: the 13F view
chapters.lede: IYE made the Insights tab on breadth: 5 tracked funds held it at June 30, up from 4 a year earlier, although total 13F value is only about $13M. It also had the best performance among the energy ETFs that passed the filters.

blocks.html: Read this one carefully: every position is tiny, under 0.01% of each fund's book, and all five holders are quant or multi-strategy firms. These are most likely trading, hedging or sector-tilt positions rather than conviction bets. The Insights tab doesn't require conviction holders for ETFs for this reason.

chapters.title: Future outlook: opportunities & risks
chapters.lede: For an energy ETF the outlook is mostly the oil outlook. After a war-driven spike, the main question for 2027 is whether peace brings back the surplus everyone expected a year ago, or whether supply risk keeps prices high.

blocks.note: The gray bars are forecasts made before the 2026 conflict. They show how far off consensus oil calls can be.

opp: If Hormuz disruption or tanker strikes return, prices could spike again. That is the upside case for producers.
Disciplined producers at $80–95 oil generate very large cash flows, which fund buybacks and dividends.
Energy often holds up when inflation surprises, which can diversify a stock portfolio.
AI data centers and LNG exports support long-term US gas demand.
Exxon and Chevron's refining and chemicals businesses soften the hit when crude falls.
Energy stocks typically trade at lower earnings multiples than the market, even after the rally.
risk: A durable Iran deal plus OPEC+ adding barrels could drive oil back toward pre-war forecasts of $55–65.
Brent lost about 16% in one week in November, and IYE is about 12% off its high.
About 40% of the fund is in two stocks.
0.38% is high for a sector ETF, and cheaper energy ETFs track similar baskets.
EV adoption and efficiency gains cap long-term oil demand growth.
The 13F interest comes from tiny quant positions, not conviction buying.

items: Peace holds, OPEC+ returns barrels, and Brent falls to $60–65. Energy gives back most of its 2026 gains.
Oil drifts toward Goldman's $78. Earnings fall from peak levels and IYE drifts lower but keeps paying its dividend.
Brent stays at $80–90 with occasional supply scares, and IYE earns its dividend plus modest gains.
The conflict simmers, shipping risk keeps a premium in prices, and producers keep up large buybacks.
A new Hormuz disruption sends Brent back above $110, and energy leads the market again.
The single biggest driver of the oil risk premium.
Decisions on returning more supply in 2027.
IEA / EIA / OPEC oil market reports
IEA's Q4 2026 supply forecast already leans bearish.
Their 2027 spending and buyback plans affect about 40% of the fund.
A cold winter would support gas-weighted producers.

glossary: Exchange-traded fund: a basket of securities that trades on an exchange like a single stock.
The annual fee as a share of assets. 0.38% costs $3.80 a year per $1,000 invested.
An index that limits how much any single stock can weigh, so one or two giants can't dominate it completely.
A diversification cap based on US tax rules for funds: no stock above 22.5%, and stocks above 4.5% together capped at 45%.
Holdings weighted by company size, so larger companies get larger weights.
Periodic reset of index weights back within the caps.
How much of a fund is in its top names. In IYE the top 15 are about 83%.
The international crude-oil benchmark, priced from North Sea oil.
West Texas Intermediate, the US crude benchmark.
An oil company that produces, refines and sells, like ExxonMobil and Chevron.
Exploration and production companies that find and pump oil and gas, like ConocoPhillips.
Turns crude into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Refiners profit from the spread between crude and fuel prices.
Pipelines, storage and processing companies, often paid fees regardless of the oil price.
Companies that drill and equip wells for producers, like SLB.
OPEC plus allies such as Russia, which coordinate oil output.
The narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman through which a large share of world oil exports pass.
More oil produced than consumed, which pushes prices down.
The extra price traders pay for oil because supply might be disrupted.
Producers holding back on growth spending and returning cash to shareholders.
Liquefied natural gas, chilled to a liquid so it can be shipped overseas.
The US Energy Information Administration and the International Energy Agency, which publish oil market forecasts.
Cash from operations minus capital spending: what's left for dividends and buybacks.
How much an investment moves relative to a benchmark.
An asset that tends to hold value when inflation rises.
A quarterly SEC report in which investment managers with over $100M list their US-listed long equity positions, including ETFs.
Funds like Citadel, D. E. Shaw and Two Sigma that run many models or teams. Their ETF positions are often hedges.
